RQ3: To what extent has battery storage become a price-forming participant in the GB Balancing Mechanism between 2023 and 2025, and how does its role differ between system-long and system-short conditions?

Figure 1. Battery marginal participation overall and in directional price tails

Figure 1. Battery marginal participation overall and in directional price tails. Each annual line connects battery's overall share of tie-adjusted marginal weight with its share in the directionally relevant System Price tail. The bid-active panel uses the lowest 5% of annual bid-active prices (P5); the offer-active panel uses the highest 5% of annual offer-active prices (P95). Thresholds are recalculated within each year and side. Each Settlement Period contributes a total marginal weight of one across its co-marginal BMUs.

What the figure measures

The paired shares separate expansion in battery's general marginal participation from expansion in economically extreme periods. The distance between the points shows whether battery's tail participation kept pace with its broader marginal role, without requiring the reader to interpret a ratio. Using annual thresholds also prevents changing absolute price levels between 2023 and 2025 from determining which periods count as extreme.

Main result. In long-system conditions, battery's share of the bid-side P5 tail rose 0.7% → 7.2% → 19.7%, alongside overall marginal shares of 4.3% → 15.4% → 30.5%. In short-system conditions, its offer-side P95 share moved 3.5% → 17.7% → 15.7%, compared with overall shares of 6.4% → 18.4% → 27.9%. Battery participation therefore moved progressively toward the long-system lower-price tail, but not persistently toward the short-system upper-price tail.

Interpretation and limitations

Directional extreme-price representation is descriptive and should not be interpreted as causal price setting, market power or the proportion of all extreme-price periods containing a battery. It compares two attributed marginal-weight shares. Inclusive thresholds can produce slightly more than the nominal 5% or 10% of periods where System Price has a mass point. The annual P10/P90 results below provide a broader-tail sensitivity check, while pooled fixed-price thresholds test sensitivity to holding the cash threshold constant across years.

Figure 2. Fixed-ladder battery-to-replacement accepted-action VWAP gap

Figure 2. Fixed-ladder battery-to-replacement accepted-action VWAP gap. Bars compare the submitted action-price VWAP of observed battery actions with a volume-matched non-battery replacement drawn mechanically from the unused accepted-action ladder. The metric is placed on a common favourable-to-battery basis: offer-active gap equals replacement VWAP minus battery VWAP, while bid-active gap equals battery VWAP minus replacement VWAP. VWAPs use removed battery volume as weights. Positive values therefore indicate that the observed battery action had a more favourable submitted action-price VWAP than its fixed-ladder replacement under the side-appropriate convention.

What the figure measures

The common-sign gap removes the need to interpret two opposite action-price directions. On the offer side, a higher replacement price means the observed battery offer was cheaper. On the bid side, a higher battery bid means the observed battery action returned more money to NESO than the replacement bid. The chart reports the price gap itself rather than the much larger absolute VWAP levels.

Main result. The favourable offer-side gap increases from £2.07/MWh in 2023 to £10.23/MWh in 2025. The corresponding bid-side gap moves from £5.64/MWh to £10.24/MWh. By 2025, the observed battery action was approximately £10/MWh more favourable than the mechanical non-battery replacement on both sides of the fixed accepted-action ladder.

Interpretation and limitations

This is a static fixed-ladder accepted-action price comparison. It is not a recalculated System Price, a causal battery effect, consumer saving or network-feasible redispatch. The replacement construction holds the observed ladder fixed and does not model participant rebidding, unit commitment, transmission constraints or wider dispatch responses. The underlying absolute battery and replacement VWAPs are retained below so the common-sign transformation remains auditable.

Figure 3. Frequency of favourable fixed-ladder battery comparisons

Figure 3. Frequency of favourable fixed-ladder battery comparisons. Bars classify identified full-accepted-BMU comparisons as battery action favourable, no material difference or replacement favourable. Each Settlement Period contributes a total weight of one divided across its co-marginal battery BMUs, preventing periods containing several battery candidates from receiving disproportionate influence. Battery action favourable means that the side-appropriate static accepted-action cost gap exceeds £0.000001; no material difference lies within ±£0.000001; and replacement favourable is below −£0.000001.

What the figure measures

Figure 2 reports the average volume-weighted action-price gap. Figure 3 instead asks how broadly the favourable fixed-ladder comparison is distributed across identified battery-marginal Settlement Periods. It distinguishes a pervasive result from an average driven by a small number of high-gap observations.

Main result. The tie-adjusted battery-favourable share is 71% → 70% → 91% in bid-active periods and 66% → 79% → 93% in offer-active periods. By 2025, the observed battery action is favourable relative to the mechanical fixed-ladder replacement in approximately nine in ten identified Settlement Periods on both sides.

Interpretation and limitations

“Favourable” refers only to the submitted accepted-action price comparison under the fixed observed ladder. It does not mean a consumer benefit, realised saving, System Price reduction or causal battery effect. The very small replacement-favourable share is partly a feature of the monotone replacement rule, which searches the next unused non-battery actions in the relevant ladder direction. The principal contrast is therefore between a strictly favourable battery result and no material difference. Raw BMU unit-period shares are retained below to show how tie adjustment changes the reported prevalence.

Figure 4. Technology composition of the fixed-ladder replacement margin by active side

Figure 4. Technology composition of the fixed-ladder replacement margin by active side. Bars show each technology's share of tie-adjusted Settlement Period equivalents in which its BMU is the final non-battery unit reached after the removed battery volume is mechanically refilled. Each identified Settlement Period contributes total weight one across co-marginal battery BMUs. The final BMU identifies the fixed-ladder replacement margin; it does not necessarily provide all or most of the replacement volume. Technologies retain the colour language used in the preceding RQ figures.

What the figure measures

The comparison identifies which technology sits at the end of the static refill sequence, separately for system-long bid-active and system-short offer-active battery observations. It therefore characterises the heterogeneous set of non-battery margins adjacent to battery actions without claiming that batteries displace a single generic technology.

Main result. CCGT is the largest single final-margin technology on both sides, accounting for 35.9% of bid-active and 39.3% of offer-active tie-adjusted SP equivalents. It is not a majority: demand-side response, pumped storage, hydro, wind, OCGT, diesel, gas and biomass collectively account for most final replacement margins. The mix also differs by system condition, particularly for non-pumped hydro, wind, pumped storage and diesel.

Interpretation and limitations

This is a frequency distribution of final ladder positions, not replacement-energy shares. A final BMU may supply only the last fraction of the refilled battery volume. The comparison also holds the observed accepted-action ladder fixed and is not a network-feasible dispatch model. Raw leave-one-BMU counts would overweight periods containing several marginal battery BMUs; all main-text shares therefore use the Settlement Period tie adjustment.
